All topics · Statistics · Lesson 13 · C&B §2.1, worked

Functions of a random variable, worked out line by line

One sitting, about 35 minutes, no new reading. Every derivation from §2.1 written out with the reason for each line, full solutions to the questions that went wrong last time, and a fresh question of the same shape after each one.

How this lesson works

Lesson 12 moved too fast, and the book skips lines in §2.1 that matter. Here every derivation is written out in full. Each line ends with its reason in brackets: [g decreasing], [chain rule], [X continuous]. When you write a proof, those brackets are what "justify each step" means: one short phrase naming the fact that makes the line true.

There's no new reading. If you want the book open, keep pp. 50–55 of Casella & Berger nearby: Theorem 2.1.3 and Example 2.1.4 on p. 51, Theorem 2.1.5 on p. 51, (2.1.11) on p. 52, Theorem 2.1.10 on p. 54.

Each part has the same shape: a fully worked derivation, then a new question with different numbers. Formula boxes take expressions (*, /, ^, sqrt( ), exp( ), log( ) = natural log). Afterwards, say honestly whether you knew each answer or guessed.

Part 1 · Theorem 2.1.3 and 2.1.5, every line (about 8 minutes)

From the reading (pp. 50–51), with the skipped lines filled in.

Setup for the whole lesson: \(X\) is continuous with pdf \(f_X\) and cdf \(F_X\); \(\mathcal X = \{x : f_X(x) > 0\}\) is its support; \(Y = g(X)\) and \(\mathcal Y = g(\mathcal X)\) is the support of \(Y\). In this part \(g\) is monotone on \(\mathcal X\), so it has an inverse function \(g^{-1}\) on \(\mathcal Y\).

Increasing \(g\). Fix \(y \in \mathcal Y\).

$$ \begin{aligned} F_Y(y) &= P(Y \le y) && \text{[definition of a cdf]}\\ &= P(g(X) \le y) && \text{[}Y = g(X)\text{]}\\ &= P(X \le g^{-1}(y)) && \text{[apply } g^{-1}\text{ to both sides; it is increasing, so } \le \text{ stays } \le\text{]}\\ &= F_X(g^{-1}(y)) && \text{[definition of } F_X\text{]} \end{aligned} $$

Nothing here used continuity, which is why Theorem 2.1.3(a) holds for every \(X\).

Differentiate. \(F_X\) is differentiable at \(g^{-1}(y)\) with derivative \(f_X(g^{-1}(y))\) [\(f_X\) continuous there, so \(F_X' = f_X\)], and \(g^{-1}\) is differentiable [assumed in Theorem 2.1.5]. So

$$ f_Y(y) = \frac{d}{dy}F_X(g^{-1}(y)) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\cdot\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y) \quad\text{[chain rule]}. $$

Decreasing \(g\). Fix \(y \in \mathcal Y\).

$$ \begin{aligned} F_Y(y) &= P(g(X) \le y)\\ &= P(X \ge g^{-1}(y)) && \text{[apply } g^{-1}\text{; it is decreasing, so } \le \text{ flips to } \ge\text{]}\\ &= 1 - P(X < g^{-1}(y)) && \text{[complement]}\\ &= 1 - P(X \le g^{-1}(y)) && \text{[}X\text{ continuous, so } P(X = g^{-1}(y)) = 0\text{]}\\ &= 1 - F_X(g^{-1}(y)). \end{aligned} $$

The fourth line is the only place continuity of \(X\) is used. That's the "second equality" the book mentions just before Theorem 2.1.3.

Two different "continuities" appear in this section, so keep them apart. \(X\) continuous means no single point carries probability, \(P(X = x) = 0\); it licenses swapping \(<\) and \(\le\). \(f_X\) continuous is what makes \(F_X' = f_X\); it licenses the differentiation step. Theorem 2.1.5 assumes both.

Differentiate. \(f_Y(y) = -f_X(g^{-1}(y))\cdot\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\) [chain rule]. Because \(g^{-1}\) is decreasing, its derivative is \(\le 0\), so the minus sign makes \(f_Y \ge 0\).

One formula (Theorem 2.1.5). In both cases \(f_Y(y) = f_X(g^{-1}(y))\,\bigl\lvert \tfrac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\bigr\rvert\) on \(\mathcal Y\): the absolute value equals \(+\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}\) when \(g\) increases and \(-\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}\) when it decreases. Outside \(\mathcal Y\), \(f_Y = 0\).

Why the continuity line matters: last lesson's two-point question, solved. \(X\) is 0 or 1, each with probability \(\tfrac12\), and \(Y = -X\). Find \(F_Y(-1) = P(Y \le -1)\).

Directly. \(Y \le -1\) means \(-X \le -1\), which means \(X \ge 1\) [multiply by \(-1\), flip]. The only value of \(X\) that is \(\ge 1\) is 1. So \(P(Y \le -1) = P(X = 1) = \tfrac12\).

With the decreasing-case formula. \(g^{-1}(-1) = 1\), so the formula says \(1 - F_X(1) = 1 - 1 = 0\). That's wrong by exactly \(\tfrac12\), which is \(P(X = 1)\): the probability sitting on the boundary point that the fourth line above threw away. For a continuous \(X\) that point carries probability 0, and the formula is right.

Your proof, in the bracket style above (3–6 lines). \(X\) is continuous with a pdf \(f_X\) that is continuous, and \(Y = 3 - 2X\). Prove that \(f_Y(y) = \tfrac12 f_X\!\left(\tfrac{3 - y}{2}\right)\), starting from \(F_Y(y) = P(Y \le y)\). Give a bracketed reason for each line, and point out the line where you use \(P(X = \text{point}) = 0\).

F_Y(y) = P(3 − 2X ≤ y) [def] = P(X ≥ (3 − y)/2) [subtract 3, divide by −2: dividing by a negative flips ≤] = 1 − P(X < (3 − y)/2) [complement] = 1 − F_X((3 − y)/2) [X continuous: P(X = (3 − y)/2) = 0]; differentiate: f_Y(y) = −f_X((3 − y)/2)·(−1/2) = ½ f_X((3 − y)/2) [chain rule; F_X' = f_X since f_X continuous]. Got it: the flip justified by dividing by a negative (or "decreasing"), the continuity line identified, chain rule with the inner derivative −1/2. Can't tell: right chain, missing reasons or the continuity line. Not yet: no flip, or plugging y straight into f_X.

\(F_Y(y) = P(3 - 2X \le y)\) [def] \(= P\bigl(X \ge \tfrac{3-y}{2}\bigr)\) [divide by \(-2\): flip] \(= 1 - P\bigl(X < \tfrac{3-y}{2}\bigr)\) [complement] \(= 1 - F_X\bigl(\tfrac{3-y}{2}\bigr)\) [\(X\) continuous: the point has probability 0]. Differentiate: \(f_Y(y) = -f_X\bigl(\tfrac{3-y}{2}\bigr)\cdot\bigl(-\tfrac12\bigr) = \tfrac12 f_X\bigl(\tfrac{3-y}{2}\bigr)\) [chain rule].

Part 2 · Example 2.1.4, every line (about 6 minutes)

From the reading (p. 51). The book does this in four lines; here are all of them.

The problem. \(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\): \(f_X(x) = 1\) for \(0 < x < 1\), else 0, so \(F_X(x) = x\) on \((0, 1)\). Let \(Y = g(X) = -\log X\). Find the cdf and pdf of \(Y\).

1. Is \(g\) monotone on the support? \(g'(x) = -\tfrac1x < 0\) for \(0 < x < 1\), so \(g\) is decreasing on \(\mathcal X = (0, 1)\). It only has to be monotone on the support, not on the whole real line (where \(\log\) isn't even defined for \(x \le 0\)).

2. The support of \(Y\). As \(x\) goes from \(0^+\) to \(1^-\), \(\log x\) goes from \(-\infty\) to \(0\), so \(-\log x\) goes from \(+\infty\) to \(0\). So \(\mathcal Y = (0, \infty)\).

3. The inverse. For \(y > 0\): \(y = -\log x \iff \log x = -y \iff x = e^{-y}\). So \(g^{-1}(y) = e^{-y}\).

4. The cdf for \(y > 0\).

$$ \begin{aligned} F_Y(y) &= P(-\log X \le y) = P(\log X \ge -y) && \text{[multiply by } -1\text{, flip]}\\ &= P(X \ge e^{-y}) && \text{[}e^{t}\text{ is increasing, keep } \ge\text{]}\\ &= 1 - F_X(e^{-y}) && \text{[complement; } X\text{ continuous, so } P(X = e^{-y}) = 0\text{]}\\ &= 1 - e^{-y} && \text{[}F_X(x) = x\text{, and } 0 < e^{-y} < 1\text{]} \end{aligned} $$

The last bracket matters: \(F_X(x) = x\) only for \(x\) in \((0, 1)\), and \(e^{-y}\) is in \((0, 1)\) exactly because \(y > 0\).

5. For \(y \le 0\), \(F_Y(y) = 0\), since \(Y > 0\) always.

6. The pdf. Differentiate on each piece: \(f_Y(y) = e^{-y}\) for \(y > 0\), and 0 for \(y < 0\) (at \(y = 0\) the value doesn't matter: one point carries no probability). This is the exponential(1) pdf.

7. Check with Theorem 2.1.5. \(f_X(g^{-1}(y)) = 1\) (since \(e^{-y} \in (0, 1)\)) and \(\bigl\lvert \frac{d}{dy}e^{-y}\bigr\rvert = e^{-y}\). Product: \(e^{-y}\). Same answer.

8. Check it's a pdf. \(\int_0^\infty e^{-y}\,dy = \bigl[-e^{-y}\bigr]_0^\infty = 0 - (-1) = 1\). Always do this check: it catches a missing derivative factor or a wrong support immediately.

Adapted from Casella & Berger, Example 2.1.4, numbers changed. \(X\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\) and \(Y = -\tfrac13\log X\). Find \(f_Y(y)\) for \(y > 0\), then give \(f_Y\!\left(\tfrac12\right)\). (An expression with exp( ), or a decimal to 4 places.)

\(g^{-1}(y) = e^{-3y}\), \(\bigl\lvert\frac{d}{dy}e^{-3y}\bigr\rvert = 3e^{-3y}\), and \(f_X(e^{-3y}) = 1\) for \(y > 0\). So \(f_Y(y) = 3e^{-3y}\), an exponential with rate 3. At \(y = \tfrac12\): \(3e^{-3/2} \approx 0.669\).

Part 3 · Last lesson's Exercise 2.1(a), solved in full (about 6 minutes)

From the book's exercises (p. 76).

The problem. \(f_X(x) = 42x^5(1 - x)\) for \(0 < x < 1\), and \(Y = X^3\). Find \(f_Y\), then \(f_Y(\tfrac18)\).

1. Monotone on the support? \(g(x) = x^3\), \(g'(x) = 3x^2 > 0\) on \((0, 1)\): increasing.

2. Support of \(Y\). \(x \in (0, 1) \Rightarrow x^3 \in (0, 1)\). So \(\mathcal Y = (0, 1)\).

3. Inverse and its derivative. \(g^{-1}(y) = y^{1/3}\), and \(\frac{d}{dy}y^{1/3} = \tfrac13 y^{-2/3}\) (positive, so the absolute value changes nothing).

4. Plug \(g^{-1}(y)\) into \(f_X\): replace every \(x\) by \(y^{1/3}\). \(f_X(y^{1/3}) = 42\,(y^{1/3})^5\,(1 - y^{1/3}) = 42\,y^{5/3}(1 - y^{1/3})\).

5. Multiply by the derivative and simplify. \(f_Y(y) = 42\,y^{5/3}(1 - y^{1/3})\cdot\tfrac13 y^{-2/3} = 14\,y^{5/3 - 2/3}(1 - y^{1/3}) = 14\,y\,(1 - y^{1/3})\) for \(0 < y < 1\).

6. Evaluate. \(y = \tfrac18\) gives \(y^{1/3} = \tfrac12\), so \(f_Y(\tfrac18) = 14\cdot\tfrac18\cdot\tfrac12 = \tfrac78\).

7. Check it's a pdf. \(\int_0^1 14(y - y^{4/3})\,dy = 14\bigl(\tfrac12 - \tfrac37\bigr) = 14\cdot\tfrac{1}{14} = 1\). ✓

Three ways this goes wrong. (a) Plugging \(y\) into \(f_X\) itself, \(f_X(\tfrac18)\), instead of \(f_X(g^{-1}(\tfrac18)) = f_X(\tfrac12)\). (b) Using \(g'(x) = 3x^2\) instead of \(\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y)\). They're reciprocals at matching points, \(\frac{d}{dy}g^{-1}(y) = 1/g'(g^{-1}(y))\), so if you use \(g'\) you must divide, not multiply. (c) A negative answer: a density can't be negative, so a minus sign means a lost absolute value or a sign slip. Check the sign before submitting.

Adapted from Casella & Berger, Exercise 2.1, new density and transformation. \(X\) has pdf \(f_X(x) = 6x(1 - x)\) for \(0 < x < 1\), and \(Y = \sqrt X\). Find \(f_Y(y)\) on \((0, 1)\), then give \(f_Y\!\left(\tfrac12\right)\). (A fraction, or a decimal to 3 places.)

\(g(x) = \sqrt x\) is increasing on \((0, 1)\), \(\mathcal Y = (0, 1)\), \(g^{-1}(y) = y^2\) with derivative \(2y\). So \(f_Y(y) = 6y^2(1 - y^2)\cdot 2y = 12y^3(1 - y^2)\). At \(y = \tfrac12\): \(12\cdot\tfrac18\cdot\tfrac34 = \tfrac98\). (It integrates to \(12(\tfrac14 - \tfrac16) = 1\). A density above 1 is fine.)

Part 4 · Formula (2.1.11) for \(Y = X^2\), every line (about 7 minutes)

From the reading (p. 52), with the chain-rule lines written out.

The cdf. \(X\) continuous, \(Y = X^2\), \(y > 0\).

$$ \begin{aligned} F_Y(y) &= P(X^2 \le y) = P(-\sqrt y \le X \le \sqrt y) && \text{[}t^2 \le y \iff \lvert t\rvert \le \sqrt y\text{]}\\ &= P(X \le \sqrt y) - P(X < -\sqrt y) && \text{[subtract the left tail]}\\ &= F_X(\sqrt y) - F_X(-\sqrt y) && \text{[}X\text{ continuous: } P(X = -\sqrt y) = 0\text{]} \end{aligned} $$

Differentiate each term separately [chain rule each time]:

$$ \frac{d}{dy}F_X(\sqrt y) = f_X(\sqrt y)\cdot\frac{1}{2\sqrt y}, \qquad \frac{d}{dy}F_X(-\sqrt y) = f_X(-\sqrt y)\cdot\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\Bigr). $$

Subtract. The minus from the subtraction meets the minus from the inner derivative \(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\) and becomes a plus:

$$ f_Y(y) = \frac{f_X(\sqrt y)}{2\sqrt y} - \Bigl(-\frac{f_X(-\sqrt y)}{2\sqrt y}\Bigr) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\Bigl(f_X(\sqrt y) + f_X(-\sqrt y)\Bigr). $$

That's (2.1.11). The two terms are the two \(x\)'s that square to \(y\), each weighted by the same stretch factor \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\).

It holds for any continuous \(X\), provided \(f_X\) is continuous at \(\pm\sqrt y\) and you read \(f_X\) as 0 outside the support. When \(-\sqrt y\) is outside the support, its term is \(f_X(-\sqrt y) = 0\) and simply drops out.

Last lesson's first \(Y = X^2\) question, solved. \(f_X(x) = \tfrac32x^2\) on \((-1, 1)\), \(Y = X^2\). Find \(f_Y(\tfrac14)\).

For \(y = \tfrac14\): \(\sqrt y = \tfrac12\) and \(-\sqrt y = -\tfrac12\), both inside \((-1, 1)\), so both terms count. \(f_X(\tfrac12) = \tfrac32\cdot\tfrac14 = \tfrac38\) and \(f_X(-\tfrac12) = \tfrac38\) too.

\(\frac{1}{2\sqrt y} = \frac{1}{2\cdot\frac12} = 1\). So \(f_Y(\tfrac14) = 1\cdot\bigl(\tfrac38 + \tfrac38\bigr) = \tfrac34\). (In general \(f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\cdot 2\cdot\tfrac32 y = \tfrac32\sqrt y\) on \((0, 1)\).)

Last lesson's find-the-first-error question, solved. \(X\) uniform on \((0, 1)\), \(Y = X^2\). Writing down (2.1.11) is not an error: by the last step of the derivation above, it holds for every continuous \(X\). The first error is the next line, "both \(f_X(\sqrt y)\) and \(f_X(-\sqrt y)\) equal 1". \(-\sqrt y\) is negative, outside \((0, 1)\), so \(f_X(-\sqrt y) = 0\) and \(f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\). Check: \(\int_0^1 \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}dy = [\sqrt y]_0^1 = 1\) ✓, while the student's \(\frac{1}{\sqrt y}\) integrates to 2.

\(X\) has pdf \(f_X(x) = \frac{x + 1}{2}\) for \(-1 < x < 1\) (0 elsewhere), and \(Y = X^2\). What is \(f_Y\!\left(\tfrac19\right)\)? (A fraction, or a decimal to 3 places.)

Both \(\pm\tfrac13\) are in \((-1, 1)\). \(f_X(\tfrac13) + f_X(-\tfrac13) = \tfrac{4/3}{2} + \tfrac{2/3}{2} = 1\), and \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt y} = \tfrac32\). So \(f_Y(\tfrac19) = \tfrac32\). In fact \(f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\) on \((0, 1)\): the \(\pm\sqrt y\) parts of \(\frac{x+1}{2}\) cancel.

\(X\) is uniform on \((-1, 1)\), with \(f_X(x) = \tfrac12\) there, and \(Y = X^2\). A student finds \(f_Y\) on \((0, 1)\). Which is the first wrong step?

  1. For \(0 < y < 1\), \(F_Y(y) = F_X(\sqrt y) - F_X(-\sqrt y)\), since \(X\) is continuous.
  2. Differentiating, \(f_Y(y) = f_X(\sqrt y)\frac{1}{2\sqrt y} - f_X(-\sqrt y)\frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\).
  3. Both \(\sqrt y\) and \(-\sqrt y\) are in \((-1, 1)\), so \(f_X(\sqrt y) = f_X(-\sqrt y) = \tfrac12\).
  4. So \(f_Y(y) = 0\) on \((0, 1)\).

The derivative of \(F_X(-\sqrt y)\) is \(f_X(-\sqrt y)\cdot(-\frac{1}{2\sqrt y})\). Subtracting it gives +, not −. Correct: \(f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}(\tfrac12 + \tfrac12) = \frac{1}{2\sqrt y}\). The student's "\(f_Y = 0\)" can't be a pdf, which is the signal that a sign went wrong.

Part 5 · The probability integral transform, every line (about 9 minutes)

From the reading (pp. 54–55).

The proof when \(F_X\) is continuous and strictly increasing. Let \(Y = F_X(X)\) and fix \(0 < y < 1\).

$$ \begin{aligned} P(Y \le y) &= P(F_X(X) \le y) && \text{[}Y = F_X(X)\text{]}\\ &= P(X \le F_X^{-1}(y)) && \text{[}F_X\text{ strictly increasing, so it has an inverse, and applying it keeps } \le\text{]}\\ &= F_X(F_X^{-1}(y)) && \text{[definition of } F_X\text{]}\\ &= y && \text{[}F_X\text{ continuous from 0 to 1, so it hits } y\text{, and } F_X^{-1}(y)\text{ is that point]} \end{aligned} $$

No pdf appears anywhere. The theorem only assumes a continuous cdf, so a proof that writes \(\int f_X\) assumes more than it's given.

This is the book's proof narrowed to a strictly increasing \(F_X\). The book's version (pp. 54–55) also handles flat stretches with the inverse \(F_X^{-1}(y) = \inf\{x : F_X(x) \ge y\}\): a flat stretch carries probability 0, so it changes no probability.

Where a discrete \(X\) breaks it: line 2 already. \(X\) is 0 or 1 with probability \(\tfrac12\) each, so \(F_X\) jumps to \(\tfrac12\) at 0 and to 1 at 1. Take \(y = 0.3\). Since \(Y = F_X(X)\) is only ever \(\tfrac12\) or 1, the true value is \(P(Y \le 0.3) = 0\). Line 2 with the book's inverse gives \(F_X^{-1}(0.3) = 0\) and \(P(X \le 0) = \tfrac12\): wrong already, because its reason ("strictly increasing, so it has an inverse") is exactly what a jumping cdf lacks. Line 4 fails too: no \(x\) has \(F_X(x) = 0.3\), because the cdf skips over 0.3. A discrete cdf has neither hypothesis.

What \(Y\) actually is here. \(Y = F_X(X)\) is \(\tfrac12\) (when \(X = 0\)) or 1 (when \(X = 1\)). A uniform can't take only two values.

\(X\) takes the values 0, 1, 2 with probabilities 0.2, 0.5, 0.3, and \(Y = F_X(X)\). What is \(P(Y \le 0.5)\)? (A uniform(0, 1) would give 0.5.)

\(F_X(0) = 0.2\), \(F_X(1) = 0.7\), \(F_X(2) = 1\). So \(Y \in \{0.2, 0.7, 1\}\), and \(Y \le 0.5\) only when \(Y = 0.2\), i.e. \(X = 0\): probability 0.2, not 0.5.

Your proof (3–6 lines, bracket style). \(F_X\) is continuous and strictly increasing. Prove that \(Y = 1 - F_X(X)\) is also uniform on \((0, 1)\): show \(P(Y \le y) = y\) for \(0 < y < 1\), with a bracketed reason for each line.

P(1 − F_X(X) ≤ y) = P(F_X(X) ≥ 1 − y) [rearrange: subtract 1, multiply by −1, flip] = P(X ≥ F_X^{-1}(1 − y)) [F_X strictly increasing: applying its inverse keeps ≥] = 1 − P(X < F_X^{-1}(1 − y)) [complement] = 1 − F_X(F_X^{-1}(1 − y)) [F_X continuous, so P(X = point) = 0] = 1 − (1 − y) = y [F_X continuous and strictly increasing, so F_X^{-1}(1 − y) is the point where F_X equals 1 − y]. Got it: the flip, the inversion justified by "strictly increasing", and the complement/continuity line. Can't tell: chain right, reasons missing. Not yet: a false step, or assuming a pdf without saying so.

\(P(1 - F_X(X) \le y) = P(F_X(X) \ge 1 - y)\) [rearrange, flip] \(= P(X \ge F_X^{-1}(1 - y))\) [\(F_X\) strictly increasing] \(= 1 - F_X(F_X^{-1}(1 - y))\) [complement; continuous cdf, so no point carries probability] \(= 1 - (1 - y) = y\). (Shortcut: if \(U\) is uniform on \((0, 1)\), so is \(1 - U\).)

You want to simulate \(X\) with cdf \(F(x) = x^3\) for \(0 < x < 1\). The computer gives the uniform number \(u = 0.216\). Using \(x = F^{-1}(u)\), what \(x\) do you report?

\(x^3 = u\) gives \(F^{-1}(u) = u^{1/3}\), and \(0.216^{1/3} = 0.6\). Why it works: \(P(F^{-1}(U) \le x) = P(U \le F(x)) = F(x)\) [\(F\) increasing; \(U\) uniform].

Go deeper: what the book skims, in one list

Beyond the reading: the fine print behind the lines above.

  1. \(g^{-1}(A)\) is a set (all \(x\) that land in \(A\)), even when \(g\) has no inverse function. Only for monotone \(g\) is \(g^{-1}(y)\) one number.
  2. Monotone on the support is enough. \(-\log x\) only needs to be monotone on \((0, 1)\).
  3. Find \(\mathcal Y\) first. The formula gives \(f_Y\) only on \(\mathcal Y\). Outside it, \(f_Y = 0\), and plugging in anyway gives nonsense.
  4. \(\le\) versus \(<\) only matters when a single point can carry probability, so "\(X\) continuous" is what lets you swap them (the decreasing case, (2.1.11), the complement in a probability integral transform proof). In the transform, continuity of the cdf also does a second job: \(F_X\) takes every value in \((0, 1)\), so \(F_X(F_X^{-1}(y)) = y\).
  5. Why Theorem 2.1.5 assumes \(f_X\) continuous and \(g^{-1}\) has a continuous derivative: so the chain rule applies and \(F_X' = f_X\) at \(g^{-1}(y)\). Those assumptions exist only to make "differentiate the cdf" legal.
  6. Always integrate your answer to 1. It's the fastest check that the derivative factor and the support are right.

Wrap-up

  • The monotone formula is the cdf method plus the chain rule; the decreasing case needs continuity in exactly one line.
  • Recipe: monotone on the support? → \(\mathcal Y\) → \(g^{-1}\) and its derivative → substitute into \(f_X\) → multiply → integrate to 1.
  • \(Y = X^2\): two chain rules, and the minus signs combine to a plus; drop any term whose point is outside the support.
  • Probability integral transform: no pdf needed, and it fails for discrete \(X\) because the cdf jumps over values.

Extra practice (optional)

Problems from Casella & Berger, Chapter 2 exercises (p. 76), easiest first. Answers are in the Casella & Berger solutions manual.

  1. Exercise 2.1(c): \(Y = X^2\) with \(f_X(x) = 30x^2(1-x)^2\) on \((0, 1)\). Use the Part 3 recipe and integrate to 1.
  2. Exercise 2.2(a): \(Y = X^2\), \(X\) uniform on \((0, 1)\). You've now seen the answer, so redo it without looking, in bracket style.
  3. Exercise 2.2(b): \(Y = -\log X\) where \(X\) has the beta-type pdf given there. Same steps as Example 2.1.4.

Extra reading: Blitzstein & Hwang, Introduction to Probability, 2nd ed., §8.1 "Change of variables" (Theorem 8.1.1 and its proof, p. 369, and the warnings box after it): the same derivation in \(\frac{dx}{dy}\) notation, with the tip that you can compute \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) and take the reciprocal.

Extra article: Eric Jang, "Normalizing Flows Tutorial, Part 1: Distributions and Determinants" (2018), blog.evjang.com/2018/01/nf1.html. Normalizing flows, a family of generative models, are this exact formula applied over and over: push a simple density through invertible maps and track the derivative factor (a Jacobian determinant in many dimensions). It shows where today's change of variables shows up in machine learning.
